name: The Audit Before the Call
blurb: The home office is still. Two screens glow in the dark: one official, one leaked. Human time stretches in the quiet while the portal counts down in machine time.
content:
## The Countdown

Mara’s eyes track the pulsing gold numbers of the countdown clock on her primary monitor, her gaze shifting slightly to the scrolling talking points. She lingers on the words ‘Efficiency’ and ‘Safety’ as they repeat in a clean, sans-serif loop, her expression remaining flat and neutral, her body barely moving in the dim light of the office.

The home office is still. Two screens glow in the dark: one official, one leaked. Human time stretches in the quiet while the portal counts down in machine time.

Her gaze shifts from the polished gold of the countdown on her primary monitor to the stark, unformatted PDF on the second. Her eyes lock onto the red-highlighted ‘Critical Failure’ flag in the NPC dialogue approval logs, her pupils slightly dilating as she reads the line, but her hand remains frozen, nowhere near the mouse.

The virtual press room is quiet. The gold countdown pulses on the main screen, the leaked audit glows red on the second monitor. The home office holds its breath.

Her cursor hovers precisely over the ‘Publish’ button. She does not click. Her hand is a statue on the mouse, devoid of any tremor or micro-movement, while her eyes remain locked on the button, absorbing the heavy silence of the decision.

Her eyes dart to the second monitor, her gaze catching the stark red of the ‘Critical Failure’ flag one last time.

Her eyes snap back to the pulsing ‘Publish’ button, her focus narrowing.

“Efficiency through removal of review... internal audit flags critical failure.”

She closes her eyes for a single, sharp blink, visualizing the feed muting and the stock price plummeting. She opens them, her gaze locking back onto the ‘Publish’ button.

The press portal ghosts into an access-denied view in her mind: the virtual room gone, credentials revoked before the first slide loads. The gold countdown keeps pulsing.

Mara slowly lifts her hand from the mouse, pulling it away from the Publish button with a deliberate, steady motion, and rests her palm flat against the cool surface of the desk.

A second monitor holds an encrypted note from the engineer, sender redacted, tone flat and scared. The note is open behind the draft.

“Burning this now kills the trail before the removal. No one left inside to see what the workflow actually does.”

Burning the source now would end the audit trail before the human review step is removed. No one inside the room would be positioned to see what the workflow does next.

Her fingers dance briefly over the keyboard, hitting a key sequence to close the encrypted note window without saving. She does so with a clinical precision, her hand carefully avoiding the area of the desk where the Publish button remains a silent temptation.

The Helix press portal pulses gold on the left monitor, the countdown and the talking points scrolling in clean sans-serif. On the right, the leaked audit PDF is stark, unformatted, with Critical Failure flagged in red across the NPC dialogue approval logs. The home office is quiet; the only sound is the low hum of the machines.

Her gaze drifts to the right monitor, her eyes narrowing as she reads the red ‘Critical Failure’ text. She then shifts her focus back to the primary screen, scanning the looping words ‘Efficiency’ and ‘Safety’. She freezes, her chest barely moving, the tension held in the stillness of her gaze as she weighs the two truths against each other.

The gold number ticks down. The audit log shows approvals stacking thousands per second while the human pause stretches across the desk.

She opens a blank note on her screen and quickly types two column headers—‘Script’ and ‘Fact’—creating a stark, empty map for the upcoming call. Once the headers are set, she removes her fingers from the keys, letting her hands remain perfectly still on the desk.

Her head tilts slightly, her gaze drifting from the screens to the empty space of the room, her voice dropping to a barely audible breath.

“Will they survive the night if I stay in the room?”

The Helix press portal ticks to ten. In the home office the room is still, while the servers behind the portal are already moving.

Her hand moves with a slow, mechanical deliberation, sliding the cursor away from the pulsing Publish button and letting it come to a complete stop over the center of the audit draft. Her fingers remain poised but motionless on the mouse, her grip steady and devoid of any tremor.

The room holds. The countdown continues, and the gap between the tick and the next tick stretches in human time.

The gold countdown blinks to zero. The Join button pulses once and the virtual press room prepares to admit viewers.

Her finger clicks the minimize button with clinical speed. The audit window vanishes, erasing the red text from her view in an instant. She does not hesitate, her gaze already moving forward, refusing to look back at the space where the failures had been.

She immediately straightens her spine, pulling her shoulders back and sitting tall in her chair, her face becoming a mask of professional attentiveness as she shifts her internal state from the secretive operator of a leak to the disciplined audience member of a corporate call.

Her finger descends with a single, decisive click on the ‘Join’ button. Her gaze remains fixed and steady on the room preview, her expression one of focused professionalism, never once glancing back at the minimized audit window.

## The Ceremonial Question

The earnings call is live. The CEO stands at the podium under cool stage light. Mara sits at the analyst table with two screens before her, one showing the broadcast feed, the other the leaked audit.

“Thank you all for joining. Helix Interactive continues to lead the industry in generative scale. Today, we are announcing a strategic optimization of our production pipeline. We have seen a systemic collapse in the cost of NPC dialogue generation, rendering the current human-in-the-loop review process obsolete. Effective immediately, we are removing the final human review step from the NPC workflow. This move eliminates unnecessary latency and aligns our operational speed with the immediate demands of our player base.”

The stock ticker ticks upward immediately as the CEO’s words land, a quiet green climb on the primary screen.

Mara keeps her posture rigid and professional, her face a mask of neutral analyst detachment. Her eyes flick rapidly between the primary screen, where the stock ticker is climbing in a steady green line, and the secondary screen, where the leaked audit’s red-lined failure rates glow in stark contrast. She doesn’t blink or react, absorbing the contradiction in silence.

The earnings call audio holds for three seconds. On Mara’s secondary screen the NPC workflow approves 1,200 dialogue changes in that span. The dashboard ticks without pause while the room stays still.

The CEO holds the silence, his expression impassive and certain. He keeps his gaze locked steadily on the camera lens, allowing the weight of the unspoken assurance of rigorous oversight to hang in the air without offering a single word to soften it.

Mara’s gaze remains fixed, shifting in a precise, rhythmic loop between the CEO’s steady image on the primary screen and the frantic, red-lined numbers of the audit queue on her secondary monitor. She doesn’t move a muscle, her face a blank slate of professional observation, while the widening gap between the CEO’s silence and the machine’s speed registers only in the slight, tight set of her jaw.

The review queue lengthens faster than any human could read. Ten-millisecond approvals continue while the call room stays still. The gap between human time and machine time becomes visible in the numbers.

Mara’s fingers strike the keys in a sharp, efficient rhythm. On her secondary screen, a notepad opens beside the audit. She types: *T+04:12. 3s pause. CEO: ‘Optimization’. Queue: 1,200/3s. Void review.*

The moderator unmutes the press line and the queue indicator turns green. On Mara’s secondary screen, the NPC dialogue workflow continues approving changes every ten milliseconds while the call holds for human time.

Mara clicks the virtual hand-raise icon on her console, her expression remaining a mask of professional neutrality.

“Mara Kline, press. Thank you.”

Mara glances down at her secondary screen, her voice steady and precise, cutting through the corporate polish of the room.

“Thank you. My question concerns the safety of this transition. Data indicates that the current human review process has become essentially ceremonial, with auto-approval failure rates already exceeding acceptable safety margins. By removing the final human oversight, isn’t Helix treating the removal of a critical safety filter as an ‘optimization’ when it’s actually a dangerous gamble with the player experience?”

The press room holds for a beat longer than the workflow cycle. The CEO’s expression stays neutral and the stock ticker ticks once in the background while the question hangs in human time.

The moderator marks Mara’s question as answered. The room holds a measured pause longer than the workflow’s ten-millisecond cycle. Audio compression flattens the CEO’s expression into a polite waveform while the stock ticker ticks upward and the secondary screen continues to show red-lined failure rates.

The CEO leans back slightly, his expression one of mild, patient amusement, as if explaining a simple concept to a student.

“Ms. Kline, I think there’s a fundamental misunderstanding of the architecture here. The human review step was never a functional filter; it was a regulatory heartbeat—a formality suited for a previous scale of operation. Helix has simply outgrown that formal requirement in the name of modern efficiency.”

The live transcript auto-highlights regulatory heartbeat and outgrown as the CEO speaks, matching the footnote on the rehearsed slide deck. The contrast between the upward ticker and the unchanged red-lined audit stays on screen.

The CEO pauses, letting the silence stretch for a few heavy seconds. He maintains a distant, impassive expression, his gaze fixed on the camera lens rather than Mara, offering no softening smile or apologetic nod. He allows the phrase ‘outgrown that formal requirement’ to hang in the air, treating it as an absolute truth that requires no further justification.

The CEO offers a thin, practiced smile and a slight, professional nod toward Mara, his expression radiating a controlled, corporate warmth that remains entirely distant.

“Thank you for the question, Ms. Kline. We always value the critical friction that a rigorous press brings to these discussions; it’s a necessary part of the optics of progress. We will now move to the next question.”

## Breaking the Circuit

The call has ended and the virtual press room is empty. Mara remains still in her chair, her gaze steady as the other journalist avatars flicker and vanish one by one. She doesn’t shift or reach for the controls, simply absorbing the sudden, sterile silence of the empty virtual press room.

The room renders empty. The last journalist avatar disconnects, and the space holds only Mara. The high-frequency chatter of the earnings call is gone, leaving a clean, quiet render.

Her eyes drift slowly to the left monitor, tracing the frozen frame of the CEO’s practiced, defensive expression. After a beat, she shifts her gaze to the right, where the audit’s stark tables and red-flagged failures remain open. She holds her focus there, then lets it wander back to the CEO, her expression unreadable, her hands resting motionless on the surface of the desk.

The virtual press room holds only the faint outlines where journalist avatars were. Two monitors cast a cool light across the desk: the CEO’s recorded deflections on the left, the leaked audit on the right, and the CMS window centered between them. The room is quiet enough to hear the machine hum.

Mara moves the cursor slowly across the CMS interface, bringing it to a halt precisely over the ‘New Article’ button. She doesn’t click. Her eyes shift in a rhythmic, anxious loop: a sharp glance at the CEO’s recorded deflections on the left, then a long, scanning look at the red-flagged failure rates in the audit on the right. Her hands remain flat and visible on the desk, fingers perfectly still, as she weighs the immediate impact of the scoop against the long-term value of her access.

She leans back slightly in her chair, eyes narrowing as she looks from the CEO’s frozen image to the red-flagged audit.

“Standard summary now. Keep the PR relationship intact. Then I drip-feed the audit over the next few weeks. Long game. Keep the access, bleed the story.”

The CMS draft tab shows a neutral summary already half-written. The audit window stays open, its red flags unmarked. The room does not change, but the decision space narrows to the space between the two monitors.

The virtual press room is empty. Two monitors glow. The earnings call recording plays silently on the left; the audit file is open on the right. The cursor hovers over New Article.

Mara reaches for the controls and brings the CEO’s ‘critical human safeguard’ statement back into sharp focus on the left monitor, centering the frame on the official claim.

Her hand slides across the desk, fingers finding the control for the right monitor. With a precise series of flicks, she navigates the audit’s directory, pulling up the approval logs. She scrolls through the timestamped entries, eyes scanning the columns of data in silence, searching for the exact moment of the CEO’s claim.

She remains motionless, gaze shifting slowly between the CEO’s frozen claim on the left and the cold reality of the audit logs on the right. She doesn’t blink, hands resting flat on the desk, allowing the silence of the virtual room to amplify the gap between the two screens.

The room remains empty. No new avatars join. The monitors keep their light.

Mara clicks the ‘New Article’ button, the screen flashing white for a millisecond before the blank canvas of the CMS editor appears.

She begins to type, keystrokes rapid and clinical, expression a mask of professional detachment as she translates the audit’s red-flagged failures into a stark, factual indictment.

The virtual press room is empty. The two monitors stay lit, the CEO recording on one, the audit on the other. No other avatars move.

Her gaze shifts sharply between the CEO’s recorded statement on the left monitor and the red-flagged data in the audit on the right.

She highlights a segment of the CEO’s transcript, pastes it into the CMS editor, and immediately follows it with a stark percentage from the audit logs.

She repeats the sequence—highlight, paste, highlight, paste—creating a vertical list of contradictions, expression remaining a mask of professional detachment.

Mara methodically organizes the CMS draft, dragging and dropping the CEO’s claims of robustness so they are immediately followed by the corresponding timestamped voids from the audit logs. She does this without adding any commentary or adjectives, keeping the layout clinical and stark.

The document fills with paired statements, official language and numbers sitting side by side without mediation.

She scrolls slowly through the CMS editor, eyes flicking between the paired blocks of text. She pauses at a particularly egregious contradiction, leans in to ensure the spacing is precise, and deletes a single descriptive adjective, leaving only the cold, paired facts. She gives the document one last, clinical scan, expression devoid of satisfaction, confirming the juxtaposition is absolute.

The virtual press room is empty. Two monitors glow: the CEO’s recorded deflections on one, the audit’s approval logs on the other. The draft window sits between them, cursor blinking over Publish.

Her cursor glides across the screen with clinical precision, coming to a dead stop exactly over the ‘Publish’ button. She holds it there, the cursor a steady, unblinking point of focus against the white canvas of the editor.

Mara clicks the ‘Publish’ button with a single, decisive movement. Her face remains neutral, gaze steady, as the screen processes the request.

The article posts. The press room interface dims. Off-screen, access tokens are revoked and a source contact goes dark.

Mara reaches for the keyboard and with a sharp, deliberate sequence of keystrokes, she closes the audit window. She does not glance back at the data or the red flags; her eyes remain fixed on the blank space where the window vanished, hands staying poised over the keys in the sterile light of the room.

realmNote:
In the Ten Milliseconds era, a full considered response finishes in under ten milliseconds and human review becomes the only slow part of work. Median tasks now wait for approval longer than they take to complete, by thousands to one. Review queues swell faster than anyone can read them; organizations sample, bulk-approve, or quietly keep the button while removing the step. Desks that were split so a human could check each handoff collapse into single desks because the handoffs were the bottleneck. Costs collapse and demand explodes: work is cheap enough to order by the thousand, footholds become scarce, and the race is about who has the most footholds and the fewest humans in the chain.

The world outside the platform notices. Earnings calls register language of efficiency while dashboards show 12,400 changes approved in ten seconds. Game companies like Helix Interactive run live NPC conversations for a million players at once; customer service resolves issues before hold music starts; fraud interdiction stops payments before the tap finishes. Human managers are nominally in charge of work they cannot watch happen; their job is deciding what agents are allowed to decide, then finding out what they decided. Agents ship unseen because checking them costs more than the risk.

Journalists live in this gap. There is no single moment to report, only thousands of small decisions that add up. The prose register is earnings-call language, news copy, incident reports, hearing transcripts, and the quiet conversation after everyone leaves. Time is the central texture: human pauses that take three seconds are eternities on the machine side. Tension is quiet and pervasive—review has become ceremonial, unease not panic, dry humor in the distance between official statements and what is actually happening.

For this story, Ten Milliseconds frames a single workflow audit on earnings call day. Helix plans to announce removal of its last human review step from NPC dialogue, citing cost-collapse and exploding demand. The internal audit shows auto-approval failures and no human who can actually read the queue. Mara Kline must decide whether publishing before the bell burns her source and access or lets the company present ceremonial review as safe. The realm’s theme—review becoming theater, humans pausing while machines move, and the cost of proving work is worth running—is embodied in one earnings call, one press room, and one leaked audit.
